metadata.title: Claude, Nav Tieout.
metadata.subtitle: Recompute, Flag — Never Verify the NAV
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does nav-tieout mean Claude is verifying the fund's NAV is correct? Takes the skill apart to show it recomputes the LP's capital account from the NAV pack and flags disagreement — the NAV itself is never checked, only the tie-out — and names the design choice that made it a checker rather than an auditor.

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. Nav-tieout sounds like Claude proving the fund's NAV is correct. It isn't — the skill assumes the NAV pack and checks whether the LP statement agrees. Let's take it apart.

beats.narration_text: The name sells one story. Claude has a nav-tieout skill, therefore Claude is independently confirming the fund's NAV is accurate — auditing the number itself. That's the story a listener packs into the word 'tieout': an evaluation, not a comparison.

shot.new_visual_element: SOUNDS LIKE AN AUDIT OF THE NAV

production_viz.label: SOUNDS LIKE AN AUDIT OF THE NAV
production_viz.caption: that's the natural read

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery contradicting the story. The skill never touches the NAV pack. Run it on a period with a known LP-statement error and the fund's NAV components sit exactly where they started — the only thing that moves is a flag on the LP side. The NAV pack is treated as trusted input, not as a claim to be tested.

production_viz.label: NAV PACK UNCHANGED
chips: RUN ON A KNOWN LP ERROR
production_viz.caption: the NAV pack is trusted, not tested

beats.narration_text: Concrete case. The NAV pack puts the LP's capital account at four hundred four thousand. The LP statement shows four hundred thousand. Nav-tieout does one thing: it recomputes the account straight from the NAV components and flags the four-thousand-dollar gap. Notice what it did not do — it never asked whether four hundred four thousand was the right number to compute from.

The mechanism is three steps, one LP statement at a time. Recompute the capital account straight from the NAV components. Compare it to what the LP was actually sent. Flag any differences. Fixed order, no branching unless the SKILL.md explicitly permits it. That rigidity is a design choice — they optimized for auditability at the expense of any judgement in the moment.

production_viz.label: RECOMPUTE, COMPARE, FLAG
production_viz.caption: in a fixed order, every run

beats.narration_text: So this makes nav-tieout a checker, not an auditor of the fund. Here's the trade. You get the same mismatch caught the same way every time, before the statement goes out. What you give up is any question about whether the NAV pack itself is right. This works if you value catching statement errors before they ship; it fails if you need somebody verifying the fund's numbers upstream.

Back to that four-thousand-dollar gap. Nav-tieout never asked whether the NAV pack's numbers were right. It recomputed the LP's account from them, saw the statement disagreed, put a flag on that line, and stopped. What happens next — who is wrong, who fixes what — is a human decision the skill deliberately does not touch.

The logic runs both directions, and both matter. A flagged mismatch doesn't prove the LP statement is wrong — the NAV pack could be the one carrying the error. And a clean tie-out doesn't prove the fund's NAV was calculated correctly — it only proves the two documents agree. Agreement is evidence of consistency, not of truth.

Here's the carry-out. Nav-tieout doesn't check whether the fund's NAV is right — it recomputes the LP's capital account from the NAV pack and flags where the statement disagrees. The NAV itself stays untested. Recomputes and flags. Never verifies.

beats.narration_text: Try it yourself. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — it makes the model spell out the recomputation before it does it, so you see exactly which NAV-pack line items feed each LP-statement field, and what a flagged mismatch does and doesn't prove. Go deeper: ask what it would take — new inputs, new procedures — for a nav-tieout to actually verify the fund's NAV, not just its consistency with the LP statement.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm looking at a private-fund NAV pack and one LP's own capital-account statement, and I want to understand what a nav-tieout actually proves. The NAV pack is authoritative for the fund's numbers; the LP statement is what the investor was sent. Walk me through, step by step, how you'd recompute the LP's capital account from the NAV components and compare it to the LP statement — and before you do it, spell out exactly which NAV-pack line items feed the recomputation and which LP-statement fields they get compared against. Then tell me what a flagged mismatch does and does not prove, in both directions.
